newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SAMPRAS EYES EMERSON ALL-TIME RECORD.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS EYES EMERSON ALL-TIME RECORD.

text.p: Newly crowned Wimbledon champion Pete Sampras has his sights fixed on becoming the most successful player in the history of the men's game after clinching his 10th grand slam title on Sunday.

Sampras lifted his fourth Wimbledon trophy to become the fourth most successful player in the event since the grasscourt tournament was first played in 1877 and moved to within two titles of emulating Roy Emerson's all-time record of 12 grand slams.

"This is what it's all about, the major titles, and, to have won 10 by the age of 25, I never really thought that would happen," said Sampras, after beating France's Cedric Pioline 6-4 6-2 6-4 in the final.

"The more I've won recently, it's something that I've been asked about breaking the 12, and that's important to me," said the American. "As a player you want to break records, and I'm in a position that I can do that."

The world number one, who has won every major except the French Open, joined Bill Tilden as the fourth most successful player in grand slams and now trails only his idol Australia's Rod Laver and Bjorn Borg of Sweden who have 11 titles and Emerson with 12.

His fourth Wimbledon title placed him alongside Laver, Reggie Doherty and Anthony Wilding, but he is still three titles behind Wimbledon's most successful player Briton William Renshaw who picked up his seven trophies before the turn of the century.

"It hasn't really hit me yet," said Sampras, who also won the Australian Open earlier this year. "To be put in the same sentence as a Laver and those guys is something. You can't have a more flattering comparison to one of the greats of all time in Laver. This is what's important to me."
Sampras dismissed claims by former Wimbledon champion Michael Stich that his single-minded approach to the game had come at the expense of other life experiences.
"When I've done playing I've got the rest of my life to do what I want, when I'm finished at 30, or 35," said Sampras, who dropped his service only twice on the way to winning Wimbledon.
"I don't want to have any regrets when I look back at my career. This is my job and this is what I love to do."
Sampras became the oldest men's singles champion at Wimbledon since Jimmy Connors, then 30, lifted the title in 1982, but said age would not be a hindrance in his bid to overtake Emerson's record.
"Connors was still winning majors when he was in his young 30s...so as long as I stay healthy and enjoy it I'm going to keep playing," he said.
"There's no reason why I can't play at this level for many years. I feel like in the middle of my career...I'm battling against all of these guys, not history."
Sampras said he had never served better in his life, adding he was playing at new level of consistency.
"I really have no fear in the game."
